procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention made against the petitioner under sub-section (1) read with sub-section (3) of section 3 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970 (President's Act No. 19 of 1970) on January 27, 1971.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Original Jurisdiction: Writ Petition No. 307 of 1971 under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for the issuance of a writ of habeas corpus.

directions: The petitioner should be set at liberty.

issue.issue_text: Whether a ground for detention is valid if it is extraneous and does not fall under the circumstances prescribed by law for ordering detention.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
The petitioner was supplied with the grounds for his detention.
One of the grounds, referred to as 'Ground No. 1', was challenged as being extraneous.
law: The circumstances under which a person can be ordered to be detained are specifically set out in Section 3 of the Act.
If even one of the grounds for detention is extraneous, meaning it does not fall under the legally prescribed circumstances, the entire order of detention is vitiated (invalidated).
application: The Court examined 'Ground No. 1' and determined that it did not fall under any of the clauses of Section 3 of the Act, which lists the legal circumstances for detention.
Because the ground was not covered by the law, the Court found it to be 'extraneous in character' and legally insufficient to justify a detention order.
The Court noted that there was nothing to show that the detaining authority (the District Magistrate) would have issued the detention order without being influenced by this invalid ground.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since one of the grounds for detention was extraneous and not justified by law, the entire detention order was vitiated. Therefore, the Court quashed the order of detention.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of detention is vitiated if even one of the grounds is found to be extraneous or invalid, especially when it is not clear if the detaining authority would have passed the order without being influenced by that ground.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
The Supreme Court examined the grounds provided for the detention and found that one of them (Ground No. 1) was of an "extraneous character" and did not legally justify an order of detention.
law: The legal principle applied by the court is that the extraneous or invalid nature of even one of the grounds of detention is sufficient to vitiate the entire detention order.
application: The court noted that there was "nothing to show" that the detaining authority (the District Magistrate) would have passed the detention order if he had not been influenced by the facts of the invalid ground.

Since it was not possible to determine if the detention order would have been made without reliance on the extraneous ground, the court concluded that the entire order was tainted by the invalidity of that single ground.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument, holding that because one of the grounds was extraneous and it was not clear that the detaining authority would have passed the order without being influenced by it, the entire order of detention was vitiated. Consequently, the court quashed the detention order.

issue.issue_text: Whether an act can be considered extortion if there is no allegation that the person intentionally put another in fear of injury, which is an essential ingredient of the offence.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
One of the grounds for detention (ground No. 1) alleged that the petitioner had received money from a pharmacy owner.
However, this specific ground did not include an allegation that the petitioner had put any person in fear of injury.
law: The Court referred to the definition of extortion under section 383 of the Indian Penal Code.
According to this definition, a key element of extortion is to "intentionally put any person in fear of any injury... and thereby dishonestly induce the person so put in fear to deliver" property.
The Court held that intentionally putting a person in fear of injury is a "necessary ingredient" of the offence of extortion.
application: The Court analyzed the specific allegation in ground No. 1 provided to the petitioner.
It found that the allegation was missing the essential element of the petitioner intentionally putting someone in fear of injury.
Because this necessary ingredient was absent from the allegation, the act described could not legally constitute extortion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an act cannot be considered extortion if there is no allegation that the person intentionally put another in fear of injury, as this is an essential and necessary ingredient of the offence. Therefore, since the specific ground of detention against the petitioner lacked this allegation, it could not be said that the petitioner was guilty of extortion.

respondent_arguments: The facts set out in ground No. 1 were not extraneous because they constituted the offence of extortion, which justified the detention.

statutes.act_name: West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of detention is vitiated if even one of the grounds provided is extraneous in character and does not legally justify the making of the detention order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's central conclusion is that the detention order is invalid because one of the grounds used to justify it was extraneous and not legally permissible under the detention act. Since there was nothing to show that the detaining authority would have issued the order without being influenced by this invalid ground, the entire order is vitiated.
legal_tests_applied: A ground for detention is tested by whether it falls under any of the clauses of the governing statute (in this case, section 3 of the West Bengal Act) that set out the specific circumstances under which a person can be detained.

If even one of the grounds for detention is found to be extraneous or invalid, the entire order of detention is vitiated, especially when it cannot be determined that the detaining authority would have passed the order without being influenced by the invalid ground.
policy_considerations: The reasoning upholds the principle that an individual's liberty cannot be curtailed based on a detention order that is even partially supported by legally impermissible or extraneous reasons. To safeguard against the unlawful deprivation of liberty, the entire order must be quashed if the court cannot be certain that the detaining authority's decision was free from the influence of an invalid ground.
